context.concept_name: Root protection

coverage.learning_objective: Protect and stop routine use of the AWS root user

required_facts.statement: The AWS account root user has broad account authority and should not be used for routine tasks.
Protect root access with MFA and do not create root access keys; delete existing root access keys when they are no longer needed.
Review root-use and access-key evidence against the root-protection checklist, using non-root identities for routine operations.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A root-protection review is not a routine operating task performed with root. It checks that exceptional account authority is protected and that normal work uses non-root identities.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The AWS account root user has broad account authority and should not be used for routine tasks.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Protect root access with MFA and do not create root access keys; delete existing root access keys when they are no longer needed.

Review root-use and access-key evidence against the root-protection checklist, using non-root identities for routine operations.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Take the supplied root-use and access-key evidence and compare each item with the protection checklist. Confirm MFA protection in the review, note whether root access keys exist, and distinguish those keys from the non-root credentials used for routine operations. Do not create root access keys for the exercise. Existing root access keys that are no longer needed should be deleted under the approved process. Record findings against the checklist rather than using root to demonstrate ordinary resource operations. The purpose of the example is to interpret protection evidence and use the appropriate routine identity, not to explore every root-only capability.

The review should distinguish root access keys from root sign-in protection. An MFA finding answers the protection question, while the access-key evidence answers whether long-lived root keys exist and remain needed. A non-root identity used for the ordinary lab task supports the routine-use boundary. Keep these findings separate so one satisfactory item is not used to erase a problem in another item.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Broad account authority is not a reason to use root for convenience. Root should not be used for routine tasks. MFA protection and root-key hygiene belong in the protection review; ordinary operational testing belongs under non-root identities.

video_need.reason: Root protection is a short evidence checklist; no demonstration of privileged root operations is needed.

practice_anchor.objective: Review a supplied root-protection checklist alongside simulated MFA, root-use, and access-key evidence. Identify routine root use and remove simulated root access keys marked as no longer needed, without accessing a real root account.
practice_anchor.success: The completed checklist records MFA protection separately from access-key findings, flags routine root use as a violation, and identifies non-root identities for routine operations. Simulated root access keys marked as no longer needed are removed, and no root access keys are created.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied MFA status, root-use evidence, and root access-key evidence visible alongside separate checklist findings, including whether each simulated root key remains needed and its removal status.

teaching_notes: Review supplied evidence; do not introduce or perform unapproved root-only operations.

context.concept_name: Attribute an AWS change using CloudTrail evidence

coverage.learning_objective: Attribute an AWS change using CloudTrail

required_facts.statement: CloudTrail event history exposes recent management events for the selected Region; it does not represent all application activity.
Filter event history by an attribute such as event name, resource name or user name and the relevant time interval.
Inspect eventTime, eventName, userIdentity and requestParameters or resources to attribute a change to an actor, operation, target and time.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A resource setting changed during a known interval, and the operator needs evidence of the actor and operation. Start with the selected Region and management-event history rather than assuming the record covers every kind of application activity.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudTrail event history exposes recent management events for the selected Region; it does not represent all application activity.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Filter event history by an attribute such as event name, resource name or user name and the relevant time interval.

Inspect eventTime, eventName, userIdentity and requestParameters or resources to attribute a change to an actor, operation, target and time.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the supplied incident interval is 09:00 to 09:15 and identifies a resource name. Filter event history by the relevant attribute and time window, then inspect candidate events. For a matching change, read eventTime, eventName, userIdentity and requestParameters or resources. Record the actor, operation, target and time from those fields. If several nearby events exist, keep the target and operation comparison explicit rather than assigning the change to the closest timestamp alone. The example establishes attribution of an AWS management change; it does not establish the sequence of all application requests or supply application tracing.

For two candidate events in the interval, compare eventName and target evidence before assigning the change. One event may involve the same actor but a different target; another may involve the target but a different operation. Retain the event whose fields support the supplied change attribution. The record should make the actor, operation, target and event time inspectable together rather than reducing the result to a person's name.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: CloudTrail event history is not all application activity. It exposes recent management events for the selected Region. Keep that scope in the attribution record and derive the actor and target from event evidence, not from a guessed owner.

video_need.reason: A brief event-history walkthrough helps locate actor, target and time fields; the attribution procedure remains complete in text.

practice_anchor.objective: Find the event for a supplied sandbox configuration change in CloudTrail event history using the supplied Region, resource name and 09:00–09:15 interval.
practice_anchor.success: Select the supplied Region, filter by the relevant attribute and time interval, and identify the matching event by comparing its operation and target with the supplied change. Record the actor from userIdentity, operation from eventName, target from requestParameters or resources, and time from eventTime rather than choosing the closest timestamp alone.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the selected Region, event-history attribute filter and time interval visible alongside candidate events and the matching event's eventTime, eventName, userIdentity and requestParameters or resources.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce X-Ray/request tracing or infer causation beyond the supplied change evidence.

context.concept_name: Attribute workload spend using resource tags

coverage.learning_objective: Attribute AWS spend to a workload using tags

required_facts.statement: Cost-allocation tags categorize costs by resource-associated tag keys and values after activation for billing.
Activate the desired cost-allocation tag, then group Cost Explorer costs by that tag for the chosen period.
Resources without the relevant active tag can leave spend unallocated to the intended workload category.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A cost report needs to distinguish orders-workload spend from other resource spend. A resource label can support that grouping only when the relevant cost-allocation tag has been activated for billing.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Cost-allocation tags categorize costs by resource-associated tag keys and values after activation for billing.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Activate the desired cost-allocation tag, then group Cost Explorer costs by that tag for the chosen period.

Resources without the relevant active tag can leave spend unallocated to the intended workload category.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the intended tag key is Workload and an approved value is orders. Activate that cost-allocation tag, then group Cost Explorer costs by it for the supplied period. Compare the orders category with spend not allocated to the intended category. If a resource lacks the relevant active tag, do not assign its spend to orders just because its name resembles the service name. Record the chosen period and tag grouping with the result. This is attribution of billed costs using resource-associated labels, not a new estimate of what the workload ought to cost. The example shows why activation and resource tagging both matter to the intended grouping.

Separate the labeling check from the billing-category check. The resource-associated Workload value states the intended category, while the active cost-allocation grouping shows how billed spend is categorized in the selected report. An unallocated category is evidence to investigate against missing relevant active tags, not permission to redistribute its amount by guessing. Keep the report's allocated and unallocated categories intact in the finding.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A label on a resource is not by itself the billing grouping check. Cost-allocation tags categorize costs after activation. Resources without the relevant active tag can leave spend unallocated, so the intended workload category may not contain all expected spend.

video_need.reason: Seeing active-tag categories beside unallocated spend helps interpretation, but the short activation/grouping explanation is sufficient.

practice_anchor.objective: Produce an orders workload cost breakdown using supplied resource tags and observed billing evidence. Activate the Workload cost-allocation tag, select the supplied period, and group Cost Explorer costs by Workload.
practice_anchor.success: The breakdown records the chosen period and Workload grouping, reports the observed orders amount, and preserves other allocated and unallocated categories. Resources missing the relevant active tag are flagged for investigation without assigning their spend to orders based on resource names.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the Workload cost-allocation tag as active and the selected Cost Explorer period grouped by Workload, with the orders category and unallocated spend visible alongside supplied resource-tag evidence.

teaching_notes: Defer workload cost estimation; use observed Cost Explorer evidence only.

context.concept_name: Centralize structured application logs in CloudWatch Logs

coverage.learning_objective: Centralize application logs in CloudWatch Logs

required_facts.statement: A log group holds log streams with shared retention and access settings; a stream is a sequence of events from one source.
Configure the supplied log collector with the application file path, log group and stream name, and verify a known JSON event arrives in that stream.
CloudWatch Logs Insights can discover fields in JSON log events, so preserving structured event fields makes them queryable.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An application writes structured events to a supplied file, and operators need those named fields in CloudWatch Logs. Follow one known event from its file source to the intended log stream rather than checking only that a log group exists.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A log group holds log streams with shared retention and access settings; a stream is a sequence of events from one source.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the supplied log collector with the application file path, log group and stream name, and verify a known JSON event arrives in that stream.

CloudWatch Logs Insights can discover fields in JSON log events, so preserving structured event fields makes them queryable.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative orders event, the supplied JSON contains a request ID, an outcome and a timestamp. Configure the supplied collector with the application file path, intended group and intended stream name. Then verify that this known event appears in that stream with its structured fields preserved. The group provides shared retention and access settings, while the stream sequences events from a source. Named JSON fields can be discovered by Logs Insights, so preserving them supports later queries. Record the event identity and arrival location as the collection evidence. Do not claim that merely creating the group proves the collector sent the intended application event.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A log group and a log stream are not interchangeable labels. The group shares settings across streams; the stream holds a sequence of events from a source. Successful setup should include a known-event arrival check in the intended stream.

video_need.reason: Following one structured event from supplied file to the intended log stream demonstrates collection and preservation of named fields.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure a supplied, ready-to-use log collector with the orders application's supplied file path, intended log group and stream name, then ship the supplied JSON events into that group.
practice_anchor.success: The known orders event appears in the intended stream within the intended group, with its request ID, outcome and timestamp preserved. The recorded collection evidence identifies the event and its arrival group and stream.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied collector's application file path, destination group and stream alongside the destination stream containing the known orders JSON event with its request ID, outcome and timestamp preserved.

teaching_notes: Do not teach later query syntax here or redesign application logging.

context.concept_name: Change and validate a Linux service configuration after external filesystem, permissions and process/service preparation

coverage.learning_objective: Change a Linux service configuration safely on an AWS host

required_facts.statement: A configuration change needs validation of its intended effect and a defined way to return to the previous working configuration.
Identify and verify the supplied rollback files, change the supplied setting and run the supplied syntax or configuration check before activation.

Use the service’s supported reload or restart procedure to activate a valid change, then inspect status and the supplied effective-setting check; on failure restore and reactivate the saved configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A lab asks for one Linux service setting to change and supplies files for returning to the previous working configuration. Before activating anything, identify those rollback files and establish how the supplied checks will judge the change.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A configuration change needs validation of its intended effect and a defined way to return to the previous working configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Identify and verify the supplied rollback files, change the supplied setting and run the supplied syntax or configuration check before activation.

Use the service’s supported reload or restart procedure to activate a valid change, then inspect status and the supplied effective-setting check; on failure restore and reactivate the saved configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the approved change modifies a setting in the supplied service configuration. First identify and verify the supplied rollback files. Change only the supplied setting, then run the supplied syntax or configuration check before activation. For a valid change, use the service's supported reload or restart procedure. Inspect both service status and the supplied effective-setting check: the latter answers whether the intended setting took effect. If the change fails, restore and reactivate the saved configuration using the approved procedure. Keep the check results with the change record so that a restart request is not mistaken for a verified outcome. Linux filesystem, permission and service-operation preparation must already be complete; the supplied files do not replace that mastery.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Activation is not validation. A reload or restart request does not replace the syntax/configuration check before activation or the status and effective-setting checks afterwards. Returning to the saved configuration also requires reactivation, not just restoring a file.

video_need.reason: The configuration-check, activation, effective-setting verification and rollback transitions benefit from a controlled service demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Change one supplied setting in a sandbox Linux service using prepared controls and supplied rollback files. Verify the rollback files, run the supplied configuration check before activation, then activate and verify the change. Restore and reactivate the saved configuration if validation fails.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied rollback files are verified before editing, only the designated setting changes, and a passing configuration check precedes activation. Service status and the supplied effective-setting check confirm the outcome. In the supplied failure case, the saved configuration is restored and reactivated, and both checks confirm the previous working state.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the sandbox service's configuration state, supplied rollback files, pre-activation check result, activation result, service status and effective-setting result visible, including the restored and reactivated state after failure.

teaching_notes: Use supplied rollback files; do not teach backup creation, boot-startup policy or independent Bash authoring.

context.concept_name: Choose rolling, blue/green or canary delivery for stated availability and rollback requirements

coverage.learning_objective: Choose a deployment strategy from availability and rollback constraints

required_facts.statement: Rolling delivery replaces portions of the workload progressively rather than replacing all instances simultaneously.
Blue/green delivery maintains separate old and new environments and switches traffic to the new environment.
Canary delivery exposes a new version to a limited share of traffic before broader rollout.
Choose a strategy by comparing traffic exposure, available parallel capacity and the ability to return traffic to a known-good version.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A release requirement allows only limited exposure to a new version and needs a way to return traffic to a known-good version. Compare delivery strategies by their replacement and traffic behavior, not by assuming one is always safest.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Rolling delivery replaces portions of the workload progressively rather than replacing all instances simultaneously.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Blue/green delivery maintains separate old and new environments and switches traffic to the new environment.

Canary delivery exposes a new version to a limited share of traffic before broader rollout.

Choose a strategy by comparing traffic exposure, available parallel capacity and the ability to return traffic to a known-good version.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Consider three proposals for the same approved release. Rolling replaces portions progressively. Blue/green maintains separate old and new environments and switches traffic. Canary exposes the new version to a limited traffic share before a broader rollout. Compare the supplied exposure constraint, available parallel capacity and rollback requirement with each proposal. If the requirement calls for separate old and new environments, the blue/green description directly addresses that arrangement. If it calls for limited initial traffic exposure, examine the canary proposal against that limit. Record how traffic can return to the known-good version under the supplied strategy instead of declaring that the strategy name guarantees recovery. The comparison is about stated requirements, not a universal ranking.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Rolling and canary are not simply two names for the same exposure pattern. Rolling describes progressive workload replacement; canary describes limited traffic exposure before broader rollout. Blue/green additionally uses separate old and new environments and a traffic switch.

video_need.reason: Traffic exposure and old/new capacity differ across strategies; animated replacement and traffic paths clarify the comparison.

practice_anchor.objective: Select rolling, blue/green or canary delivery for a supplied service scenario and defend the choice using its traffic-exposure limit, available parallel capacity and required return to a known-good version. Use supplied strategy descriptions rather than configuring a deployment.
practice_anchor.success: The selected strategy meets the scenario's stated exposure, capacity and rollback requirements. The justification accurately describes its replacement or traffic behavior, cites the supplied return-to-known-good arrangement and explains why the alternatives are less suitable.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make progressive workload replacement, separate old and new environments with a traffic switch, and limited initial traffic exposure visibly distinct. Show each supplied proposal's parallel-capacity needs and route back to the known-good version alongside the scenario requirements.

teaching_notes: Defer product-specific rollout procedures; keep examples tied to stated exposure, capacity and rollback requirements.

context.concept_name: Collect host telemetry with the CloudWatch agent

coverage.learning_objective: Collect host telemetry with the CloudWatch agent

required_facts.statement: The CloudWatch agent collects configured host metrics and logs and sends them to CloudWatch.
In the agent configuration, choose metrics under metrics_collected and append instance-identifying dimensions such as InstanceId.
Start the agent with amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl using fetch-config, the supplied configuration location and -s, then verify the expected metric and instance dimension in CloudWatch.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A host signal should appear in CloudWatch under the correct instance identity. Use the supplied agent configuration to connect the chosen collection settings with a specific observed metric.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The CloudWatch agent collects configured host metrics and logs and sends them to CloudWatch.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
In the agent configuration, choose metrics under metrics_collected and append instance-identifying dimensions such as InstanceId.

Start the agent with amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl using fetch-config, the supplied configuration location and -s, then verify the expected metric and instance dimension in CloudWatch.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the supplied host metrics under metrics_collected and append the intended InstanceId dimension. Start the agent through amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl with fetch-config, the supplied configuration location and -s. Then locate the expected metric in CloudWatch and compare its instance dimension with the approved host. A metric from a different instance is not verification for this host, even if the metric name matches.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Starting the agent is not the same as verifying collection. Check the expected metric and instance-identifying dimension in CloudWatch; the configuration describes what should be sent, while the observed series checks the intended host.

video_need.reason: A short agent setup and metric inspection helps connect configuration with InstanceId-specific output; text covers the bounded procedure.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure the supplied agent profile on a prepared sandbox EC2 host: select the supplied metrics under metrics_collected, append the InstanceId dimension, and start the agent with amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl using fetch-config, the supplied configuration location and -s. Verify the resulting metric in CloudWatch.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied profile selects the required host metric and appends InstanceId; the agent is started using the supplied configuration location; and the expected metric appears in CloudWatch with an InstanceId matching the approved sandbox host.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the expected CloudWatch metric and its InstanceId dimension visible alongside the approved sandbox host identity so that the learner can verify both the signal and its source.

teaching_notes: Use supplied configuration and agent-control procedure; require external package and Linux service preparation.

context.concept_name: Configure CloudWatch alarm evaluation and missing-data behavior from supplied signals and thresholds

coverage.learning_objective: Configure CloudWatch alarm evaluation

required_facts.statement: A metric alarm evaluates a statistic over periods against a threshold and has OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA states.
EvaluationPeriods is the number of evaluated periods, and DatapointsToAlarm is the number of breaching datapoints required within that window.
Set the supplied metric, statistic, period, comparison operator and threshold along with the evaluation counts; compare the resulting state with the supplied samples.
Missing-data settings are breaching, notBreaching, ignore (retain current state), and missing (insufficient data when all datapoints are missing); missing is the default.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An alarm should reflect a supplied sequence of metric samples, including gaps. To explain its state, separate the statistic and threshold from the size of the evaluation window and the number of breaches required within it.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A metric alarm evaluates a statistic over periods against a threshold and has OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA states.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
EvaluationPeriods is the number of evaluated periods, and DatapointsToAlarm is the number of breaching datapoints required within that window.

Set the supplied metric, statistic, period, comparison operator and threshold along with the evaluation counts; compare the resulting state with the supplied samples.

Missing-data settings are breaching, notBreaching, ignore (retain current state), and missing (insufficient data when all datapoints are missing); missing is the default.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the approved samples for three evaluated periods are above, below and above the supplied threshold. Set EvaluationPeriods to 3 and DatapointsToAlarm to 2 for this example, alongside the supplied metric, statistic, period and comparison operator. There are two breaching datapoints in that window, matching the stated count requirement. Now examine the supplied missing-sample case with its selected missing-data policy. Do not silently treat a gap as a real zero or a real breach: use breaching, notBreaching, ignore or missing as configured. For the all-missing case, missing yields insufficient data; ignore retains the current state. Compare the resulting state with the supplied cases and retain the settings with the sample evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: EvaluationPeriods is not the number of breaches required. It is the number of evaluated periods; DatapointsToAlarm supplies the required breach count. Also, missing is the default missing-data setting, not a promise that every isolated gap immediately produces INSUFFICIENT_DATA.

video_need.reason: A sequence of sample windows, breach counts and missing-data states makes alarm evaluation behavior substantially clearer.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure one metric alarm with the supplied metric, statistic, period, comparison operator, threshold, EvaluationPeriods, DatapointsToAlarm and missing-data policy. Evaluate supplied complete-sample and all-missing windows to verify state transitions.
practice_anchor.success: The saved configuration matches the supplied settings. For complete-sample windows, the resulting OK or ALARM state matches the required breach count. For all-missing windows, breaching yields ALARM, notBreaching yields OK, ignore retains the supplied current state, and missing yields INSUFFICIENT_DATA.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show successive supplied evaluation windows with period samples, threshold comparisons, breach counts, configured evaluation counts, missing-data policy, prior state and resulting state. Distinguish missing samples from real zero values and include complete-sample and all-missing cases.

teaching_notes: Use supplied signals and thresholds; do not introduce unsupported sparse-data evaluation rules.

context.concept_name: Configure secure human access with temporary credentials

coverage.learning_objective: Grant secure human AWS access using IAM Identity Center

Use the supplied Identity Center assignment workflow to assign the approved user or group, account and permission set, then sign in to that account and test the intended access.
Configure a named SSO profile with aws configure sso and establish a session with aws sso login --profile NAME rather than storing long-lived IAM user keys.

teaching_blocks.content: An operator needs approved human access without saving long-lived IAM user keys. Use the supplied Identity Center assignment and sign-in workflow, then test the access represented by the assignment.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: IAM Identity Center permission sets define permissions made available through assignments to users or groups in specified AWS accounts.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied Identity Center assignment workflow to assign the approved user or group, account and permission set, then sign in to that account and test the intended access.

Configure a named SSO profile with aws configure sso and establish a session with aws sso login --profile NAME rather than storing long-lived IAM user keys.

media.group_title: From an account assignment to permission-set sign-in

context.concept_name: Configure security groups after external ports/firewall preparation

coverage.learning_objective: Configure AWS security-group rules to enforce required workload flows and an approved ingress baseline

required_facts.statement: Security groups contain allow rules for traffic evaluated at associated network interfaces; they have no explicit deny rules.
Security groups are stateful: response traffic for an allowed connection is allowed regardless of rules in the response direction.
Add inbound rules specifying the required protocol, port range and approved source, remove unnecessary ingress, and test the required connections and their responses.

misconceptions.statement: Using a security-group ID as an allowed source does not import the referenced group’s rules into the destination group.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A sandbox service should accept only its approved connection traffic. Build the required allow rule from the protocol, port range and source, then test the connection and its response. Apply the external ports/firewall preparation before this AWS rule exercise.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Security groups contain allow rules for traffic evaluated at associated network interfaces; they have no explicit deny rules.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Security groups are stateful: response traffic for an allowed connection is allowed regardless of rules in the response direction.

Add inbound rules specifying the required protocol, port range and approved source, remove unnecessary ingress, and test the required connections and their responses.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the supplied service requires TCP port 443 from an approved source range. Add that inbound allow rule on the associated security group and remove unnecessary ingress. Test the required connection and its response. For an allowed tracked connection, the response is allowed regardless of rules in the response direction because security groups are stateful. Keep the test about traffic the security group actually evaluates: Amazon-provided DNS and instance metadata traffic are not filtered by security groups. If the approved source is a security-group ID, it does not import that group's rules into the destination group. Use the supplied source and destination roles rather than widening ingress to make an unexplained test pass.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Security groups contain allow rules, not explicit deny rules. Also, a referenced source group does not contribute its own rule list to the destination group. Do not generalize the connection tests to traffic that security groups do not filter.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content:
Security groups do not filter traffic to Amazon-provided DNS or EC2 instance metadata services.

Using a security-group ID as an allowed source does not import the referenced group’s rules into the destination group.

video_need.reason: A tracked request/response flow and source-group reference diagram clarify stateful behavior and filtering exceptions.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure one EC2 workload security group using a supplied approved baseline requiring TCP port 443 from an approved source range. Add the required inbound rule, remove unnecessary ingress, and use supplied connection tests to verify the required connection and its stateful response.
practice_anchor.success: The security group associated with the workload network interface admits TCP port 443 from the approved source range and contains no unnecessary inbound rules. Supplied tests confirm that the approved connection and its response succeed without a separate response-direction allow rule, while a new connection from an unapproved source is not admitted.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show an approved TCP port 443 connection evaluated at the workload's associated network interface and its tracked response allowed regardless of response-direction rules. Distinguish a new connection from an unapproved source. Show that a source-group reference identifies an allowed source without importing that group's rules, and mark Amazon-provided DNS and instance metadata traffic as outside security-group filtering.

teaching_notes: Keep DNS/IMDS filtering exceptions explicit; do not imply security groups filter every AWS-service flow.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Declare resource "aws_instance" "NAME" with ami, instance_type and subnet_id set to the supplied values.

Run terraform init to install providers, terraform plan to inspect intended changes, and the approved terraform apply step to create the instance; verify the instance settings.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Replace APPROVED_VERSION in the provider declaration with the exact approved version. In the supplied aws_instance resource, use the supplied AMI, instance type and subnet ID; NAME is the declaration's chosen resource label. Run terraform init for provider installation, then terraform plan to inspect the intended instance changes. teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence

live_code.observable_success: The completed HCL contains an exact provider pin and the supplied ami, instance_type and subnet_id. Initialization installs the provider, the inspected plan proposes one matching instance, and the created instance's settings match after the approved apply step.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the exact provider pin visible alongside the aws_instance declaration, then align its AMI, instance type and subnet ID with the supplied specification, planned instance settings and verified live instance settings.

context.concept_name: Evaluate resource-based permissions for a requested operation

coverage.learning_objective: Evaluate AWS resource-based permissions

required_facts.statement: A resource-based policy is attached to a resource and specifies the principals, actions and resources covered by its statements.
For an S3 bucket policy, compare Principal, Action, Resource and Condition with the caller’s request; bucket and object ARNs identify different resource scopes.
Same-account identity and resource permissions can contribute allows, but applicable explicit denies override them; cross-account access generally requires permission on both sides.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A caller's request reaches an S3 resource with a bucket policy. Evaluate the resource-side statement against that particular caller and target rather than treating an identity-policy allow as the whole resource-permission explanation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A resource-based policy is attached to a resource and specifies the principals, actions and resources covered by its statements.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
For an S3 bucket policy, compare Principal, Action, Resource and Condition with the caller’s request; bucket and object ARNs identify different resource scopes.

Same-account identity and resource permissions can contribute allows, but applicable explicit denies override them; cross-account access generally requires permission on both sides.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Take a supplied object request and compare its caller with Principal, its operation with Action, its object ARN with Resource and its request values with Condition. A bucket ARN and an object ARN identify different scopes, so a statement about the bucket is not automatically a statement about that object request. For a same-account example, identity and resource permissions can contribute allows, but an applicable explicit deny overrides them. For the supplied cross-account example, keep the qualification that access generally requires permission on both sides. Record the matching scope and applicable deny evidence without turning that general cross-account rule into an exhaustive account of every special case.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A resource policy is attached to the resource and includes principal scope; it is not simply an identity policy moved to another file. Also, an applicable explicit deny still overrides contributed allows. Keep bucket and object ARN scopes distinct.

video_need.reason: Caller and bucket/object scope diagrams clarify resource-policy matching, cross-account qualifications and explicit-deny precedence.

practice_anchor.objective: Evaluate one supplied S3 bucket policy against object requests from approved and unapproved callers. Select the matching Principal, Action, Resource and Condition evidence, then use supplied identity-permission and explicit-deny evidence to determine whether each request is permitted.
practice_anchor.success: For each request, correctly identify which policy fields match, distinguish bucket scope from object scope, and record the permission outcome. An applicable explicit deny overrides allows; same-account permissions can contribute allows, while cross-account access generally requires permission on both sides.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the caller-to-resource relationship visible: distinguish the bucket ARN from object ARNs, connect request values to Principal, Action, Resource and Condition, and show how same-account allows, applicable explicit denies and permissions on both sides of a cross-account request affect the outcome.

teaching_notes: Preserve generally for cross-account requirements; avoid advanced grant exceptions not in this brief.

context.concept_name: Execute Python AWS automation in an isolated dependency environment after active registry language preparation

coverage.learning_objective: Execute Python AWS automation in an isolated environment

required_facts.statement: A virtual environment isolates the Python interpreter context and installed packages used by an application.
Create one with python -m venv ENV_DIR and activate it using the platform’s activation command, such as source ENV_DIR/bin/activate on Unix.
Install supplied dependencies with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt inside the environment, inspect them with python -m pip list, and run the supplied script with that interpreter.
Confirm the approved AWS profile and Region through the supplied credential configuration before running AWS automation.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Python automation script has a requirements file. Before running it against AWS, prepare an isolated dependency environment and confirm the intended operator context.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A virtual environment isolates the Python interpreter context and installed packages used by an application.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create one with python -m venv ENV_DIR and activate it using the platform’s activation command, such as source ENV_DIR/bin/activate on Unix.

Install supplied dependencies with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt inside the environment, inspect them with python -m pip list, and run the supplied script with that interpreter.

Confirm the approved AWS profile and Region through the supplied credential configuration before running AWS automation.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case

Run the supplied script with that environment's interpreter only after confirming the approved AWS profile and Region through its credential configuration. practice_anchor.objective: Create and activate one virtual environment, install and inspect the supplied dependencies, confirm the approved AWS profile and Region, and run the supplied automation script with that environment's interpreter.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied script runs with the activated environment's interpreter after dependency inspection and AWS context confirmation, without installing packages into the host's global Python environment.

live_code.required_skill: Execute the supplied Python automation using an isolated interpreter and dependency context.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide the supplied automation script, requirements.txt, an environment directory name, the platform's activation command, and supplied credential configuration identifying the approved AWS profile and Region. Begin with no project virtual environment active; script editing is not required.
live_code.observable_success: One virtual environment is created and activated; dependencies are installed and listed through its interpreter; the supplied credential configuration is checked against the approved profile and Region before execution; the supplied script outcome and environment/context used are recorded. Global Python packages remain unchanged.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the active virtual environment, environment-scoped dependency installation and package list, and separate approved AWS profile and Region confirmation visible before the supplied script executes.

context.concept_name: Extract structured AWS CLI inventory across paginated results

coverage.learning_objective: Extract AWS CLI inventory across pagination

required_facts.statement: The AWS CLI automatically follows service-side pagination for supported commands unless automatic pagination is disabled.
Use an explicit --profile and --region with --output json for structured inventory and avoid --no-paginate when the full listing is required.

--page-size changes service-call page size rather than the total output count; --max-items limits output and a returned NextToken must be resumed with --starting-token when manually collecting the remainder.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An inventory task needs all results in one approved account and Region. Page controls affect how results are retrieved or bounded, so read them before claiming that a listing is complete.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The AWS CLI automatically follows service-side pagination for supported commands unless automatic pagination is disabled.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use an explicit --profile and --region with --output json for structured inventory and avoid --no-paginate when the full listing is required.

--page-size changes service-call page size rather than the total output count; --max-items limits output and a returned NextToken must be resumed with --starting-token when manually collecting the remainder.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Run the supplied supported inventory command with explicit profile and Region and JSON output. For the full listing, keep automatic pagination enabled rather than adding --no-paginate. If the exercise deliberately uses --max-items to collect a bounded portion, retain the returned NextToken and resume with --starting-token for the remainder. Changing --page-size adjusts service-call page size; it is not the same as limiting total output with --max-items. Keep the continuation evidence with the inventory.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A smaller page size does not mean a smaller total inventory. Distinguish service-call page size from the output limit, and do not discard a continuation token when manually collecting the remainder.

video_need.reason: A brief page-size/output-limit comparison helps interpret continuation tokens; the bounded pagination rules are fully stated in text.

media.group_title: How automatic pagination builds a complete inventory

segments.label: How the AWS CLI collects a full listing across service pages
segments.summary: A supported listing operation can require several service requests rather than one. Using an EC2 snapshot listing as the example, the speaker explains that each response indicates whether more results remain. The AWS CLI automatically requests subsequent pages until the service reports no more results, then assembles the complete list in memory and returns it as command output.

bridge_note.before: Watch how service responses tell the AWS CLI whether another page is needed, and how automatic pagination assembles those pages into one listing.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains automatic collection, but not disabling it, explicit profile/Region/JSON settings, or page-size, output-limit, and token-resumption controls. The text covers those requirements for a complete, consistently scoped inventory.

practice_anchor.objective: Export one sandbox resource inventory using a supplied supported AWS CLI inventory command with explicit --profile, --region, and --output json. Keep automatic pagination enabled for the full listing, then use a bounded exercise to practise retaining a returned NextToken and resuming with --starting-token.
practice_anchor.success: The full-listing export uses the supplied sandbox profile and Region consistently and does not use --no-paginate or an output limit. In the bounded exercise, the learner preserves each returned NextToken, resumes in the same context until no continuation remains, and distinguishes --page-size from --max-items.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make successive service requests and responses visible, showing automatic collection until no results remain alongside a bounded --max-items result whose NextToken is passed to --starting-token. Keep the same explicit profile and Region visible throughout, and distinguish service-call page size from total output count.

teaching_notes: Apply pagination only to supported commands; do not invent an inventory command or API continuation format.

context.concept_name: Hand over an actionable operational runbook

coverage.learning_objective: Hand over an actionable runbook

required_facts.statement: A runbook documents procedures for a known operational outcome and should be usable by the operator performing the task.
Write the task’s preconditions, ordered actions and expected results so execution can be checked rather than inferred.
Include failure-handling and escalation instructions identifying when routine execution must stop and who takes over.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Another operator must perform a known task without relying on your memory. A useful runbook makes the conditions for acting and the evidence for advancing explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A runbook documents procedures for a known operational outcome and should be usable by the operator performing the task.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Write the task’s preconditions, ordered actions and expected results so execution can be checked rather than inferred.

Include failure-handling and escalation instructions identifying when routine execution must stop and who takes over.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For a supplied restart task, write its preconditions, approved ordered actions and expected results from the established procedure. Include the condition that stops routine work and name the escalation recipient. Read the draft as the receiving operator: can each expected result be checked before advancing? Replace an instruction such as confirm it worked with the supplied observable result. Do not invent a recovery action outside the approved procedure.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A list of actions alone is not an actionable runbook. Preconditions, expected results and failure/escalation instructions are needed so the operator can check execution rather than infer success.

video_need.reason: The handoff is a short document structure and expected-result check; a sample runbook table suffices.

practice_anchor.objective: Produce one bounded runbook for a supplied restart task using its established procedure and owner information. Document the outcome, preconditions, ordered actions, checkable expected results, failure-handling instructions, stop condition and escalation recipient.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted runbook lets another operator identify when the task may begin, which approved actions occur in order, how to check each expected result, when routine execution must stop and who takes over. It introduces no actions outside the supplied procedure.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make a sample restart runbook visible with its outcome and preconditions, followed by ordered action rows showing expected results, failure-handling instructions, stop conditions and escalation recipients.

teaching_notes: Use established procedures and owners; defer live incident execution to the later runbook-recovery concept.

context.concept_name: Operate an EKS Pod using supplied cluster-access setup

coverage.learning_objective: Inspect and operate an EKS Pod

required_facts.statement: A Pod groups containers with shared networking and storage and has a lifecycle distinct from the controller that may replace it.
Pod phases include Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown; phase alone is not a complete diagnosis of container health.
Use kubectl get pod NAME, kubectl describe pod NAME and kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER to inspect status, scheduling or runtime events and container output.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied EKS workload has a Pod that appears to be running. The operator still needs evidence about its containers and events. Pod phase is one lifecycle observation, not a complete health diagnosis.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Pod groups containers with shared networking and storage and has a lifecycle distinct from the controller that may replace it.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Pod phases include Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown; phase alone is not a complete diagnosis of container health.

Use kubectl get pod NAME, kubectl describe pod NAME and kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER to inspect status, scheduling or runtime events and container output.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Using the supplied cluster access setup, substitute the approved Pod name into kubectl get pod NAME. Record its phase, then inspect kubectl describe pod NAME for scheduling or runtime events. Use kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER for the intended container's output. Suppose the phase reads Running while the supplied events and logs show a container problem. Preserve those observations together rather than deciding that Running settles health. A Pod groups containers with shared networking and storage; its lifecycle is distinct from a controller that may replace it. This exercise inspects the Pod and its container output, not the controller's desired-replica reconciliation or cluster administration.

If the Pod is Pending, use its described scheduling events as evidence rather than applying a correction inferred from the phase label alone. If it is Running, inspect the intended container's runtime events and output. The same inspection sequence accommodates different phases because it records what happened at the Pod and container boundaries. An unrelated container's output is not evidence about the one named in the exercise.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Running is a Pod phase, not a complete diagnosis of container health. Other phases include Pending, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown, but the phase list does not replace inspection of events and the intended container's logs.

video_need.reason: Pod phase, runtime events and container logs are separate changing observations that benefit from a live inspection demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Inspect one seeded failing Pod using the supplied cluster access and image. Substitute the supplied Pod and container names into kubectl get pod NAME, kubectl describe pod NAME and kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER, then identify the failure supported by the observations.
practice_anchor.success: Record the Pod phase, relevant scheduling or runtime events, and the intended container's output. Identify the seeded failure using those observations together, without treating Running as proof of container health or changing the workload.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied Pod's status, described events and intended container's logs together, making the distinction between Pod phase and container failure evidence visible.

teaching_notes: Use supplied cluster access; leave Deployment reconciliation and self-managed cluster administration out of scope.

coverage.learning_objective: Operate an RDS managed database

required_facts.statement: An RDS DB instance has an identifier, engine, endpoint and operational status that can be inspected in the console or through describe-db-instances.
Inspect the intended DB instance and verify its engine and status before attempting the supplied database connection.
Connect using the supplied endpoint, database client and approved credentials, then run the supplied query to check the data marker; instance status alone does not verify application data.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A managed database is available for an approved connection test. Verify the intended instance and the data marker separately; a resource status does not answer whether the expected application data is present.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An RDS DB instance has an identifier, engine, endpoint and operational status that can be inspected in the console or through describe-db-instances.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the intended DB instance and verify its engine and status before attempting the supplied database connection.

Connect using the supplied endpoint, database client and approved credentials, then run the supplied query to check the data marker; instance status alone does not verify application data.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Locate the supplied DB instance identifier in the console or describe-db-instances result. Record the instance identity and endpoint with the safe query outcome so the test can be tied to the intended database. teaching_blocks.content: An acceptable instance status does not verify application data. The instance inspection checks identity, engine and status; the supplied connection and query check the data marker. Neither result should be used as a substitute for the other.

practice_anchor.objective: Inspect the supplied sandbox RDS instance using preconfigured networking. Verify its identifier, engine and operational status before connecting with the supplied endpoint, database client and approved credentials, then run the supplied query to check the expected data marker.
practice_anchor.success: The recorded identifier matches the intended instance, its engine and status are compared with the supplied requirements, and its endpoint is recorded. The supplied query result is compared with the expected data marker, with the data-check outcome reported separately from instance status.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the intended RDS instance's identifier, engine, operational status and endpoint visible alongside the supplied query result and expected data marker, distinguishing resource inspection from application-data verification without exposing credentials.
